## TL;DR

Mission Control and Stories now use one representative content block, so neither route creates an arbitrary multi-card grid or a wrapped extra row while the repository loads. The shell owns the 180 ms show delay and 350 ms minimum visible duration. Per-view loading remains conditional on the absence of usable data, which keeps cached snapshots visible during refresh. I also made the non-board placeholder counts explicit in one shared map and added a rendered count assertion for every skeleton kind, with board counts checked against their real column definitions.

## Work and rationale

The mismatch came from using a generic `dashboard` collection shape for Mission Control. Its actual page is a continuous dashboard with usage, status cards, automation, timeline, feed, decisions, and attention panels. A generic six-card grid did not represent that composition and, because it used auto-fit, its geometry changed with viewport width. The shell skeleton now uses one dashboard block in a single column. This communicates that the data area is loading without pretending that each dashboard panel is an independent card collection. Stories is a vertical list of variable-height story cards, so the loading state uses one representative row rather than inventing a full set of stories. The static page heading remains in the shell above either placeholder.

The shell coordinates first-load behavior centrally. It waits 180 ms before exposing a skeleton, so fast initial fetches do not flash a placeholder. If the repository becomes ready after the skeleton appears, the shell keeps it visible until 350 ms have elapsed. During that time it retains the same page header and content region. The view-level guards continue to require the absence of loaded data before showing their local skeletons; silent refreshes therefore do not erase existing content. The shell marks its loading content region busy and the skeleton exposes one polite status label rather than making each decorative bar an announcement.

For count consistency, Work and Inputs use `WORK_BOARD_COLUMN_COUNT` and `INPUT_BOARD_COLUMN_COUNT`, the same definitions used by their board layouts. The remaining shapes have named counts in `LOADING_SKELETON_ITEM_COUNTS`, consumed by `PageSkeleton` and exercised through mounted component assertions. This makes the intentionally minimal counts reviewable and prevents accidental differences between the declared count contract and rendered placeholders. The dashboard and row kinds explicitly have one representative block. Cards, table rows, targets, and deployment summaries retain compact representative counts appropriate to their different content structures.

The audit covered every route in `LOADING_SKELETON_ROUTES` and the view-local skeleton call sites. Results:

| Page | Real content layout | Skeleton shape | Audit result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mission Control (`/`) | Continuous responsive dashboard: usage, six status tiles, automation, multi-panel data | One dashboard block | Corrected; avoids the former auto-fit card pile |
| Work | Six status columns, collapsing to one column on narrow screens | Board columns using shared count | Matches column count; mobile is one column |
| Client board | Three project status columns | Input board using shared count | Matches column count |
| Inputs | Three workflow columns | Input board using shared count | Matches column count |
| Stories | Vertical list of variable-height story cards | One row | Corrected; one realistic representative row |
| Checks | Plan and recent runs in table-like sections | Table | Reasonable compact table placeholder |
| Agents | Settings cards and agent/budget content | Cards | Compact cards; local loading only while config is unavailable |
| Releases | Release status cards, then channel distribution | Cards | Status and distribution each use cards while empty |
| Deployments | Environments and status data | Deployment summary plus matrix | Shape follows the environment summary/table grouping |
| Dev | Declared runnable targets in target cards | Targets | Matches the target-card layout |
| Secrets | Environment/secret rows | Table | Matches row-oriented data |
| Settings | Configuration sections and aligned rows | Rows | Minimal row placeholder; page chrome remains visible |
| Repo Context | Document/context list | Rows | Minimal row placeholder |

Animation remains a low-contrast 2.4 second pulse, with the existing reduced-motion media rule disabling it. No additional animation preference was introduced. The UI rebuild is required after this UI change and the scoped RepoOS check is the final gate.

## Approaches tried

I traced the shell route map, its timing watcher, real dashboard composition, Stories list markup, board column definitions, and every `PageSkeleton` call site. I retained the shell-level route replacement because it already provides static headings during repository initialization and avoids duplicating delay timers in individual views. I kept local skeletons for independently fetched views because they have real loaded-data guards and do not participate in the repository-wide shell transition.

I considered representing the dashboard with multiple skeleton panels, but that would repeat the original problem in a less obvious form: dashboard panels are heterogeneous and their exact responsive layout depends on real content. One quiet placeholder block gives a stable first-load footprint without implying false panel geometry. For Stories, one row is similarly more honest than guessing how many story cards will exist.

## Challenges and blockers

The existing shot fixture catalogue had no way to hold the shell on the corrected first-load views. I added two explicit fixtures, `loading:dashboard` and `loading:stories`, and wired them to hold the app shell on the corresponding skeleton while preserving the route's normal heading. The task now declares a loading-state shot for each route using those fixtures and a targeted highlight. These are deterministic preview fixtures; they do not alter ordinary app loading behavior.

## Key learnings

Loading placeholders are part of responsive layout, so auto-fit is risky when it is not tied to the page's actual columns. The board pages already provide a useful precedent: share the layout's column definition instead of guessing in the skeleton. For heterogeneous data pages, one representative block is often clearer than a full fabricated page. Finally, route-shell loading and view-local loading have different lifecycles; keeping the delay/minimum duration in the shell while preserving each view's existing loaded-data guard avoids bringing placeholders back during background refreshes.
